messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 63

**The Space Between the Door and the Window**

Mei Lin is fifty-one years old, a dentist with her own practice in a mid-sized city, a woman who has spent nearly two decades building something steady and her own. She is precise by nature — her patients describe her as calm, reassuring, someone whose hands never shake. That steadiness is what makes it so disorienting, she says, that she cannot seem to find it anymore outside the walls of her operatory.

Three years ago, a former patient began leaving notes at her clinic. At first they seemed like ordinary expressions of gratitude — handwritten cards, small gifts left with the receptionist. Then the notes changed in tone. They became intimate, then possessive, then threatening. The man began appearing outside her building. He followed her to her car. He sent messages to her home address, which she had never given him, which meant he had found it himself. For fourteen months, Mei Lin lived inside the slow-motion terror of not knowing where he would appear next. She filed police reports. She changed her routes to work. She installed cameras. She did everything she was told to do, and still he came. The stalking ended only when he was arrested for an unrelated offense and subsequently incarcerated. Legally, it was over. For Mei Lin, it was not.

She describes the period during the stalking as one of radical shrinking — she stopped going to the farmers' market she had loved, stopped walking her neighborhood in the evenings, stopped feeling that any space was truly hers. Now, even with him behind bars, the shrinking has not reversed. She knows, intellectually, that he is gone. She does not feel it. When she pulls into her clinic's parking lot each morning, she scans every car before she gets out of her own. She notes which patients are new. She has memorized the face of every man who has come within ten feet of her in the past year, and she cannot explain why, only that her body insists on it.

At work, she functions. The dental chair, the instruments, the familiar choreography of procedure — these things hold her. But between patients, when the room is quiet, her mind goes somewhere she does not choose to go. She replays the moment she found a note tucked under her windshield wiper in a parking garage, the specific quality of the fluorescent light, the smell of exhaust, the way her hands went cold. The memory arrives without invitation and leaves her standing at her sink, gloved hands dripping, unsure how much time has passed.

Her husband, David, has been patient and frightened in equal measure. He tells her she is safe now. She nods. She cannot make herself believe him, and she has stopped trying to explain why. At night she sleeps lightly, waking at sounds that do not warrant waking — a car door, the neighbor's dog, the house settling into itself. She has moved her side of the bed closer to the wall, though she has not told David that this was a deliberate choice. She does not want him to know how much of her is still back in that parking garage.

She has begun avoiding professional conferences, worried about being in unfamiliar cities, in hotels with corridors she does not know. She has declined two speaking invitations this year. Her world, like her sleep, has grown shallow and narrow.

What troubles Mei Lin most is not the fear itself but the feeling that she has become a stranger to her own competence. She can numb a jaw, extract a root, calm a frightened child in her chair. She is good at her work. And yet she cannot walk to her own mailbox after dark without her heart climbing into her throat. She wants to know, she says, when she gets to stop being afraid of a man who is no longer there.
